title: Education Dempsey, Patrick If You're Banning AI You Got a Lot of Explaining to Do
author: Dempsey, Patrick
summary: No one has definitively figured out AI in education yet, and Dempsey argues that educators who claim otherwise -- on either side of the debate -- are projecting false confidence onto an open question. He proposes two honest frameworks: the AI-Free Zone, where an instructor deliberately restricts AI to protect a specific human capacity they can name; and the AI Experiment Zone, where an instructor accepts students already have access and treats that reality as something to learn from together. The AI-Free Zone carries a higher burden of explanation -- banning a tool increasingly embedded in how people think and work requires the educator to articulate precisely what human capacity is being protected. Dempsey argues that most educators cannot defend their assignments without leaning on inherited assumptions: the exam became a proxy for mastery, the essay became a proxy for critical thinking, and when AI threatens the proxy, everyone acts as if it threatens human development itself.
points: * Confidence on either side of the AI debate is premature: no one knows for certain whether AI is a net positive or negative for learning, which means confident bans and endorsements are both forms of intellectual dishonesty. * The AI-Free Zone requires educators to articulate precisely what human capacity they are protecting -- attention, memory, close reading, the ability to sit with confusion long enough for thought to become one's own -- and why restriction is the right method. * Most assignments are inherited proxies assumed to develop certain capacities, but the link between proxy and capacity is often assumed rather than demonstrated: 'Exam = mastery' becomes sacred until AI threatens it. * The AI Experiment Zone assumes only that attentive educators can learn something valuable by watching what changes when students work with these tools available. * Educators who are comfortable with ambiguity and willing to relinquish control may be uniquely positioned to help shape what good teaching and learning look like in the AI era.
quotes: Nobody has figured out AI in education yet. Of course, we are trying. We are getting better. We are using sound theory and practical experiments to start defining 'good.' But no one knows ... yet.
Given that we don't know for sure, I see only two real options for educators: the AI-Free Zone and the AI Experiment Zone.
The AI-Free Zone is the space where an instructor intentionally restricts or prohibits AI because they believe its use would interfere with the development of some specific human capacity.
If you want to live in the AI-Free Zone, the challenge is to name what you are protecting.

The truth is, educators mostly start with inherited assignments that become familiar assignments, that become preferred assignments, which we then assume worked because some students produced acceptable artifacts.
The assignment becomes a proxy for human development. Then the proxy becomes sacred. Then AI threatens the proxy, and everyone acts as if it threatens the human development itself.
The only assumption we have is that we can learn with students if we are comfortable with a little ambiguity and a lot of relinquishing control.
